Learning Objectives
Identify important anatomic considerations for the meniscus.
Describe the manner in which meniscal microstructure and composition contribute to the
function of the meniscus.
Explain the manner in which the meniscus responds to injury and its biologic limitations with
regard to healing and repair.
Review common repair enhancement techniques and emerging biologic augmentation
strategies for the management of meniscal injury.
Overview
The medial and lateral menisci of the knee are crescent-shaped fibrocartilaginous structures
that possess a triangular cross section that increases femorotibial contact areas.

The meniscus is a vital component for the normal function and long-term health of the knee
joint, increasing stability to femorotibial articulation, distributing axial load, absorbing shock,
and providing lubrication to the knee joint.1
A large portion of adult knee pain results from underlying osteoarthritis, and meniscal tears
are among the most common factors contributing to the progression of knee osteoarthritis.2,3
Meniscal preservation is protective against the development and progression of arthritis.4
The vascularity of the meniscus affects the healing of meniscal repairs.
Understanding the menisci on a molecular and biomechanical level enables greater knowledge
and awareness of preservation and protection from injury.
Advancements in surgical techniques and biologic augmentation have expanded the
indications for meniscal repair to include tear patterns previously considered irreparable.5
Embryologic Development
Differentiation occurs within the limb bud from mesenchymal tissue.
Meniscal size relative to tibial coverage remains fairly consistent throughout maturation.
Vascularity gradually recedes to its peripheral origin to supply only 10% to 30% of the menisci
by age 10 years.
Cellularity declines as collagen content increases.

Embryologic Development
By 14 weeks of gestation, the menisci arise from a condensation of the intermediate
layer of mesenchymal tissue to mature into their typical anatomic shape.6,7 The medial
meniscus covers approximately 60% and the lateral meniscus 80% of the corresponding
tibial plateau, and this proportion remains consistent throughout development.8 During
development, the vascularity arising from the periphery initially extends throughout the
meniscal width but gradually decreases to supply only the peripheral 10% to 30% of the
meniscus by age 10 years.8 In addition, meniscal cellularity declines while collagen
content increases and organizes in a circumferential fashion.6


Meniscal Stability
The knee menisci are wedge-shaped fibrocartilaginous structures situated between the
femoral condyles and the tibial plateau. The macrostructure of the meniscus is divided
into its tibial attachments at the anterior and posterior roots, the curved anterior and
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:43 PM
AAOS | Meniscus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002002
9/44

posterior horns, and the meniscal body at its midportion.6The medial meniscus has a
semicircular shape that covers approximately 50% to 60% of the medial tibial plateau in
adulthood.1 The posterior horn is a mean of 11 mm in the anteroposterior dimension,
whereas the anterior horn is narrower.10 The anterior horn of the medial meniscus
attaches to the tibia anterior to the ACL near the intercondylar fossa with considerable
variability. The anterior intermeniscal, or transverse, ligament connects the anterior
horns of the medial and lateral menisci. The posterior root attachment lies in the
posterior intercondylar fossa between the lateral meniscus and the PCL.11 In addition to
its root attachments, the meniscotibial (coronary) ligament stabilizes the medial
meniscus through its attachment from the inferior aspect of the posterior horn to the
tibia. Peripherally, the medial meniscus is firmly attached to the deep medial collateral
ligament and the joint capsule, limiting its mobility6,11 (Figure 8). The lateral meniscus is
an oblong, circular shape with symmetric sizes of the anterior and posterior horns. The
lateral meniscus anterior root attaches anterior to the intercondylar eminence and just
lateral to the ACL insertion site on the tibia (Figure 9), whereas the posterior root
attaches posterior to the lateral tibial spine just anterior to the medial meniscus
posterior root.1 The popliteomeniscal fascicles extend from the lateral meniscus to the
posterior capsule to create the popliteal hiatus. The meniscofemoral ligaments are
variably present structures that connect the posterior horn of the lateral meniscus to the
medial femoral condyle. These are described by their relative relationship to the PCL,
with the ligament of Humphrey crossing anterior to the PCL and the ligament of
Wrisberg posteriorly from knee extension to flexion6,12 (Figure 10).


Vascular Anatomy
The blood supply of the menisci arises from the superior, middle, and inferior (medial
and lateral) geniculate arteries as they branch from the popliteal artery.13,14 Synovial
artery branches supply the anterior and posterior root attachments, whereas synovial
and capsular artery branches form a perimeniscal capillary network to supply the
peripheral 10% to 30% of the meniscus15 (Figure 15). From the anterior and posterior
horns, endoligamentous vessels branch into the substance of the menisci to perform
terminal loops and provide direct nutrition over a short distance.16 The remaining
central portion of the meniscus occupies an avascular zone that receives its nutrition
from the synovial fluid via loading diffusion.17 Accordingly, menisci have three zones that
can be discerned based on vasculature and extracellular matrix (ECM) composition.
These zones are commonly described as white/white, red/white, and red/red zones.6
Figure 15 Gross images of sectioned cadaver knee specimens after injection of the
vasculature with India ink and fixation in formalin show the blood supply to the
meniscus. A, A 5-mm-thick frontal section of the medial compartment of the knee
(Spalteholz, magnification ×3) shows branching radial vessels from the perimeniscal
capillary complex (PCP) penetrating the peripheral border of the medial meniscus. F =
femur, T = tibia. This image demonstrates a sagittal view of meniscal vascularization.
Superior aspect of the (B) medial and (C) lateral menisci after vascular perfusion with
India ink and tissue clearing via a modified Spalteholz technique show the vascularity at
the periphery of the menisci and at the anterior and posterior horn attachments. The
absence of peripheral vasculature at the posterolateral corner of the lateral meniscus
(arrow) represents the area of passage of the popliteal tendon. (Reproduced with

Neural Anatomy
The nerve supply is similar to the vascular supply (concentrated in the periphery of the
meniscus).
Mechanoreceptors supply proprioceptive feedback during joint motion.
Three types of mechanoreceptors have been identified: Ruffini endings, Pacinian corpuscles,
and Golgi tendon organs.
Sensory fibers play a role in pain production.

Neural Anatomy
The posterior articular branch of the tibial nerve innervates the knee along with
contributions from the terminal branches of the obturator and femoral nerves. In
addition, the recurrent peroneal branch of the common peroneal nerve supplies the
lateral portion of the capsule. Nerve fibers enter the capsule and the peripheral portion
of the menisci along a similar path as the blood supply. The highest nerve density lies in
the anterior and posterior meniscal horns, whereas the peripheral third of the body has
greater innervation than the middle third18 (Figure 16).

Figure 16 Illustrations show controversial innervation of the meniscus described by
Wilson (left) and Kennedy-Alexander (right).
Three types of mechanoreceptors have been identified in the human meniscus. Ruffini
endings are type I mechanoreceptors, which have a low threshold and adapt slowly to
pressure and joint deformation. Pacinian corpuscles (type II mechanoreceptors) have a
low threshold but adapt quickly to alterations in tissue tension. Golgi tendon organs
(type III mechanoreceptors) have a high signal threshold and exist in a greater
concentration in the posterior horns, where they play a role in neuromuscular inhibition
as the knee reaches terminal flexion.6,19
Microstructure and Composition
The meniscus is a dense ECM composed of water, collagen, cellular elements, proteoglycans,
and glycoproteins (Resource 1).
Water

Cellular distribution: predominantly fibroblast-like cells in the superficial layer and

Make up 75% of the ECM dry weight and function to provide the primary structural
framework
90% type I collagen with small contributions of collagen types II, III, V, and VI collagen
Collagen fibers are arranged in a specific superficial to deep manner that facilitates the

Middle (deepest) layer

ligamentous connections of the meniscal horns to the tibial articular surface.
Radially oriented tie fibers secure circumferential (longitudinal) fibers in place.


Microstructure and Composition
The human meniscus is a well-organized structure consisting of fibrochondrocytes
dispersed among a dense ECM. As the predominant meniscal cell type,
fibrochondrocytes serve to produce and maintain the ECM20 (Figure 21). The
fibrochondrocytes in the superficial layer of the meniscus appear similar to fibroblasts
with their fusiform shape, whereas those in the deeper portion of the meniscus are
more ovoid and chondrocyte-like.21 To aid in matrix production function,
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:43 PM
AAOS | Meniscus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002002
24/44

fibrochondrocytes contain abundant endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi complexes,
whereas a paucity of mitochondria suggests energy production occurs via anaerobic
glycolysis.6,22
Figure 21 Transverse histologic sections obtained from the outer two-thirds of the
menisci of cadaver model knee specimens at ×100 (A) and ×400 (B) shows the fibers (CF)
running along the length of the meniscus, with the radial fibers (RF) radiating in various
directions (light microscopy; hematoxylin-eosin). The arrows in panel B show cells that
appear elongated or spindle-shaped in single rows. (Reproduced with permission from
Gupta M, Goyal PK, Singh P, Sharma A: Morphology of intra-articular structures and
histology of menisci of knee joint. Intl J Appl Basic Med Res 2018;8[2]:96-99.)
Water contained within the ECM accounts for 65% to 75% of the overall meniscal weight
and volume.1 The posterior areas of menisci have an increased water content compared
with the central and anterior portions. The remainder of the meniscus is composed of
organic material. Composing 75% of the dry weight, collagens are the predominant ECM
component and function to provide tensile strength to the meniscus.24 Type I collagen
comprises most of the collagen content, with small contributions of types II, III, V, and VI
collagen.22 Random collagen fiber orientation in the most superficial layer of the
meniscus provides tensile strength and resistance to shear forces. In the deeper layers,
the type I collagen fibers are organized to run circumferentially within the meniscus
parallel to its peripheral border. The circumferentially oriented fibers are bound
together by interspersed radially oriented tie fibers providing structural support1,25
(Figure 22). This organization allows for the conversion of vertically oriented
compressive forces into circumferential hoop stresses distributed throughout the
meniscus.6,21
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:43 PM
AAOS | Meniscus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002002
25/44

Figure 22 Schematic cross-sectional diagram of the meniscus shows the circumferential
arrangement of collagen fibers and radial tie fibers. (Reproduced with permission from
Jacob G, Shimomura K, Krych AJ, Nakamura N: The meniscus tear: A review of stem cell
therapies. Cells 2020;9[1]:92.)
Matrix proteins other than collagen account for 8% to 13% of meniscal dry weight.1
Fibronectin is a matrix protein involved in cellular processes, such as cell
migration/adhesion and tissue repair, whereas elastin likely contributes to tissue
resiliency.22 Proteoglycans are large negatively charged molecules consisting of one or
more glycosaminoglycan side chains covalently bonded to a core protein. These
hydrophilic molecules exist within the ECM and contribute to 1% to 2% of the dry weight.
Aggrecan is the most abundant proteoglycan found in the human meniscus, which
accounts for its viscoelastic compressive properties. Decorin, biglycan, and fibromodulin
are smaller proteoglycans found in the meniscus with unclear importance.21 In addition
to providing the meniscus with its viscoelastic ability to resist compressive forces,
proteoglycans play an important role in the hydration of meniscal tissue. The meniscal
horns and inner 50% of the weight-bearing meniscus contain the highest concentration
of glycosaminoglycan side chains.26 The most common glycosaminoglycans in the adult
meniscus include chondroitin-6-sulfate (40%), chondroitin-4-sulfate (10% to 20%),
dermatan sulfate (20% to 30%), and keratin sulfate (15%).6,24,27

Functions
Load transmission
The menisci improve joint congruity between the rounded femoral condyles and the flat
tibial plateau.9
They increase the contact area between tibial and femoral articulation, decreasing contact
pressures on the articular cartilage.
The posterior horns of the menisci transmit approximately 50% of weight-bearing load in full
leg extension; this increases to 85% at 90° of flexion.
Shock absorption (Figure 23)
The menisci disperse axial loads via elongation of their circumferential fibers (hoop stresses).
The firm anterior and posterior root attachments allow hoop stresses to be absorbed
without meniscal extrusion.
The biphasic nature of the meniscus allows for absorption of compressive loads through
movement of water within the matrix of meniscal fibrocartilage.
Joint stability
The medial meniscus is a secondary stabilizer against excessive anterior translation in ACL-
deficient knees.
The posterior horn of the medial meniscus acts as a wedge to prevent excessive anterior
translation of the tibia.
Joint lubrication
Helps distribute synovial fluid across the articular surfaces
Joint nutrition
Menisci absorb and then release synovial fluid nutrients for the cartilage.
Proprioception
Nerve endings provide sensory feedback for joint position sense.

Figure 23 Illustration shows how force is transduced on and throughout the knee meniscus. The
free-body diagram shows the forces acting on the knee meniscus during loading (only the lateral
meniscus is shown). During everyday activity, the menisci are compressed by the downward force
of the femur (Ffem). Because the meniscus is a wedge, the femoral force is enacted at an angle;
therefore, a vertical component (Fv) exists, which is countered by the upward force of the tibia
(Ftib). In addition, a horizontal component (Fh) of the femoral force exists, which is exerted
radially (Frad) outward on each meniscus. The horizontal force is, in turn, countered by the
anchoring force of the attachments at the posterior and anterior horns of the meniscus (Fpost
and Fant, respectively). In addition, as this compression occurs, circumferential stress (Fcir) is
created along the meniscus. Therefore, the menisci function by converting compressive loads to
circumferential tensile loads. At the same time, shear forces are developed between the collagen
fibers within the meniscus while the meniscus is deformed radially. (Reproduced with permission
from Makris EA, Hadidi P, Athanasiou KA: The knee meniscus: Structure-function,
pathophysiology, current repair techniques, and prospects for regeneration. Biomaterials

During knee flexion from 0° to 120°, the menisci translate in the anteroposterior dimension
to account for femoral roll back.
The mean medial translation of the menisci is 5.1 mm; the mean lateral translation of the
menisci is 11.2 mm.
The difference in translation is the result of better bony conformity of the medial
compartment and greater fixation of the medial meniscus than the lateral meniscus to the
joint capsule.
Meniscectomy
Load transmission
Partial meniscectomy results in a proportionate increase in contact stress.
Total meniscectomy decreases the femorotibial contact area by 50%, which increases
articular cartilage contact pressures by 100% with a medial meniscectomy and by 200% to
300% with a lateral meniscectomy.
Shock absorption—Total meniscectomy reduces the shock absorption capacity of the knee
by at least 20%.
Joint stability—Medial meniscectomy increases anterior translation of an ACL-deficient knee.
Combination of increased shear forces and compressive loads is thought to result in arthritic
changes28 (Figure 24).

Although previously believed to be a vestigial structure of the knee,29 the meniscus has
multiple important biomechanical functions crucial to the normal function of the knee.
The menisci increase the contact area and congruity, in turn decreasing contact stresses,
across the tibiofemoral joint.30 In addition, shock absorption, load transmission, stability,
nutrition, joint lubrication, and proprioception are vital functions provided by the
meniscus.1
The load-bearing function of the meniscus occurs as axial weight-bearing forces through
the knee are converted to tensile forces along the circumferential collagen fibers of the
meniscus.31 The firm anterior and posterior root attachments allow these hoop stresses
to be absorbed without meniscal extrusion.32 Studies have demonstrated that 50% of
the load through the medial compartment and 70% of the lateral compartment load
transmission occur through the menisci.33 The compressive loads through the posterior
horns increase during knee flexion, from 50% in extension to 85% transmission in 90° of
flexion.30 Medial meniscectomy reduces the femoral condyle contact area by 50% to
70% and increases contact stress by 100%, whereas total lateral meniscectomy
decreases contact area by 40% to 50%, with a resultant increase in lateral compartment
contact stress by 200% to 300% of normal.34,35 A normal knee demonstrates a shock-
absorbing capacity approximately 20% higher than knees that have undergone
meniscectomy.31 The clinical importance of these alterations was highlighted in a study
by Pengas et al,36 which demonstrated a statistically significant increase in osteoarthritis
and a 132-fold likelihood of total knee arthroplasty in a cohort of adolescent patients at a
mean follow-up of 40 years after total meniscectomy.6,36
The menisci contribute to joint stability because the concave superior meniscal surface
increases the congruity between the convex femoral condyles and the relatively flat tibial
plateaus. This stabilizing effect has been best demonstrated in ACL-deficient knees, in
which medial meniscectomy has been reported to increase anteroposterior tibial
translation by more than 50% with the knee in 90° of flexion.37 The posterior horn of the
medial meniscus is the most essential structure to resisting anterior tibial force in the
ACL-deficient knee.38 The lateral meniscus acts as a secondary stabilizer against rotatory
and valgus loads during pivot shift maneuvers in ACL-deficient knees.6,39

The menisci are thought to contribute to the nutrition and lubrication of the knee;
however, the mechanism for this has not been fully elucidated. Bird and Sweet40 used
scanning electron microscopy to demonstrate a system of micro-canals within the
meniscus that communicated with the synovium. These canals have been postulated to
provide fluid transport for nutrition and joint lubrication. The menisci may reduce
frictional forces via compression of synovial fluid into the articular cartilage. In addition,
mechanoreceptors located within the anterior and posterior meniscal horns provide
joint proprioception. The rapidly adapting Pacinian corpuscles relay joint motion,
whereas the slowly adapting Ruffini endings provide joint position sense.6,41

Response to Injury
Vascular proliferation from adjacent soft tissues within the knee joint is vital to the reparative
response of the meniscus (Resource 2).
Meniscal lesions contiguous with the adjacent synovial blood supply can heal spontaneously,
whereas injuries isolated to avascular portions have tenuous healing potential (Figure 25).

Provides improved long-term outcomes compared with partial meniscectomy
Protective against the development and progression of arthritis
Biologic augmentation strategies attempt to promote chemotaxis, cellular proliferation, and/or

Abrasion of the adjacent synovium or trephination of the meniscus has been proposed to

The intra-articular inflammatory changes that occur after meniscal injury have been
investigated in multiple studies, with a particular focus on the risk of future
osteoarthritis.44-46 Similarly, the vascular response to meniscal injury has been
extensively studied in animal models,47-50 showing that vascular proliferation from
adjacent soft tissues within the knee joint is vital to the reparative response of the
meniscus. Injuries to the meniscus that occur within the peripheral one-third exist within
the vascularized portion of the meniscus (red/red zone) and may undergo a healing
response. Postinjury, an initial inflammatory response is quickly followed by the
formation of a fibrin clot. Undifferentiated mesenchymal stem cells migrate to the zone
of injury from the vasculature. A new matrix is produced, and healing occurs via the
formation of fibrous scar tissue.51 With regard to the timeline for meniscal healing, a dog
model previously demonstrated meniscal repair tissue attaining 80% of original strength
at 12 weeks postinjury.6,52
Conversely, meniscal injuries within the inner one-third (white/white zone) or the middle
one-third (red/white zone) have limited capacity for healing given the avascularity of the
tissue. Therefore, meniscal healing is thought to be dependent on an adequate blood
supply. The potential role of blood flow in the meniscal healing process likely is related
to the delivery of nutrients and oxygen, the infiltration of the affected site with cells
pertinent to tissue repair, and the formation of blood clots and release of tissue
remodeling mediators.48,49 Several studies have investigated the effects of
immobilization on the vascular response to meniscal injury. Immobilization was shown
to inhibit the normal increase in blood flow observed in response to meniscal injury and
may decrease synovial fluid production and tissue nutrition.53,54
Given the poor healing response throughout the avascular meniscal tissue, a great deal
of research has been directed toward biologic adjuvants (Video 1).

The evidence for the use of biologics for joint preservation in meniscal repair has been
studied.5 The earliest adjuvant was synovial abrasion with the use of a meniscal rasp to
increase vascular response and trephination of the peripheral meniscus and capsule.51
Because of the improved meniscal healing rates in patients undergoing concomitant ACL
reconstruction, bone marrow stimulation techniques have been used during meniscal
repair to release bone marrow–derived mesenchymal cells.55 The direct application of
PRP and/or pluripotent stem cells has been investigated in animal and human studies,
with variable results.56-58 Several stem/progenitor cell sources are actively being
investigated for their therapeutic healing effects, which have been observed in animal
models and tissue explant models of meniscus injury and repair. Cell sources include
mesenchymal progenitor/stem cells from adipose, synovium, cartilage, and bone
marrow. Cell-based therapies are promising and are being used alone and in
combination with growth factors and scaffolds in preclinical settings to optimize
efficacy6,23 (Figure 29). Advancements in surgical techniques and biologic augmentation
have expanded the indications for meniscal repair to include tear patterns previously
considered irreparable.
